Prime Minister David Cameron yesterday held a historic meeting with Iranian President Hassan Rouhani on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, as he seeks to inject new momentum into efforts to find a political solution to the Syria conflict. The meeting, which lasted around an hour, was the first between the leaders of their countries in over a decade, with ties between the UK and Iran having been strained since the 1979 Islamic revolution. Cameron and Rouhani discussed a range of issues, including Iran's role in mediating a peaceful resolution to the conflict in Syria, as well as the need to tackle the spread of Islamic State (IS) across the Middle East. The UK has long urged Iran to use its influence with its allies, including the Syrian regime, to bring about a peaceful resolution to the conflict, which has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and displaced millions more. In a statement after the meeting, a Downing Street spokesperson said that Cameron had " emphasised the importance of international co-operation in countering threats from IS and addressing the humanitarian crisis in Syria". The spokesperson added that the Prime Minister had also stressed the need for "a more inclusive and representative government" in Syria, which would "guarantee the rights of all citizens". The Iranian leader, speaking at a press conference, hailed the meeting as a "new chapter in British-Iranian relations" and said that he believed there was " great potential" for further co-operation between the two countries. Rouhani added that Iran was committed to finding a peaceful solutions to the conflict in Syria, and saw the UK as a key partner in such efforts. Cameron's efforts to secure a breakthrough on Syria are seen as crucial, with the conflict now entering its fifth year and with little sign of a resolution in sight. The Prime Minister has faced criticism in the past for his handling of the conflict, with many arguing that the UK's decision to provide limited military support to rebels aligned with the moderate opposition had made little difference. In recent days, however, there have been signs of a new effort by the international community to find a peaceful solution to the conflict. The US Ambassador to the UN, Samantha Power, has floated the idea of a new UN peacekeeping mission for Syria, while sources close to the British government have suggested that the UK may be willing to provide greater military support to rebels in the coming months.

Scottish Government solicitor-general Alison Di Rollo QC yesterday told MSPs on Holyrood's Constitution, Europe and External Affairs Committee that it would be a "serious breach of convention" if the UK government were to exclude Scottish Parliament representation from Brexit talks. As it currently stands, the Scottish Government has been excluded from negotiations on the final stage group remaining in the single market and customs union, drawing the ire of First Minister Nicola Sturgeon. Ms Sturgeon has repeatedly called on the UK Government to permit representation from the devolved nations, or for a Scottish-French deal to be reached. Yesterday, Ms Di Rollo reinforced the First Minister's stance, arguing that exclusion from talks would undermine the already strained relationship between the UK and Scottish Governments, and the constructive relationship which needs to be fostered post-Brexit. "The convention that the Scottish Government should be consulted by the UK government on matters of UK and EU and EEA policy that affect Scotland is an important constitutional requirement," she noted. "Excluding Scotland from Brexit talks would therefore be a serious breach of that convention. "If the UK government takes decisions on Brexit which do not reflect the views of all four countries, that would have very serious implications for the heart of our constitutional relationship." Her intervention follows days of tension between the Scottish and UK Governments, with the First Minister growing increasingly vocal about the need for devolved nations to be included in key Brexit talks. Yesterday, Ms Sturgeon, called out her counterpart Boris Johnson, accusing the Conservative leader of being "hostile" towards the devolved Scottish Parliament and insisting that the First Minister, and the assemblies at Cardiff and in Belfast, must be involved in shaping the UK's exit from the EU. "It's almost as if Boris Johnson thinks he's immune from criticism," she said. "In reality, his inability to deliver on Brexit is looking increasingly manifest. "Instead of trying to throw Scottish devolution into reverse gear, he and the UK Government should be focusing on maintaining the critical relationships we need for Scotland to succeed outside the EU." With the prospect of runs on succession talks emerging, Ms Di Rollo hit out at the UK Government for undermining public confidence in its ability to deliver on Brexit. "The current proposals exclude Scotland from negotiating membership of the single market and customs union," she said. "That does not enhance the public confidence we all wish to see."

Scottish Justice Minister Humza Yousaf has welcomed a report showing that waiting times for trials in Scotland's courts are being reduced, but lawyers claim more action is needed to tackle delays which have led to criticism of the overburdened justice system. The latest SCTS data, covering the period from August 2020 to July 2022, reveals that the average time from first appearance to final disposal dropped from 499 days (or nearly 16 months) to 249 days, bringing it closer to the Scottish Government's target. Lagos: The Endless Hustle of Africa's Largest City As the sun rises over the bustling metropolis of Lagos, the daily grind begins. It's a cacophony of horns, chatter, and industry, a sensory overload that is both exhilarating and exhausting. Stand anywhere in this vibrant city and you can see the thunderous traffic, which gives Lagos an energy and intensity quite unlike any other. Cars, buses, motorbikes, and pedestrians weave a complex dance, each one trying to outmaneuver the others in a relentless pursuit of progress. From the crowded streets of Surulere to the sleek skyscrapers of Victoria Island, every inch of Lagos seems to be pulsating with life. The city's inhabitants, known for their resilience and entrepreneurial spirit, have adapted to the challenges of an overpopulating metropolis. They navigate treacherous roads on decrepit motorcycles, using their wit and bravado to outsmart the chaos that surrounds them. The city's infrastructure may be strained, but its people are anything but. Lagos is a place where the air is thick with opportunity, where the rules of law and order are often bends to suit the needs of those who inhabit it. It's a city of traders and market stall-holders, of artisans and musicians, all vying for a space in the world's attention. Yet, beneath the surface, Lagos has a beauty that is hard to ignore. In the evenings, as the sun dips into the horizon, the city's lights come alive, casting a golden glow over the crowded streets. It's a time for families to gather, for friends to share meals, and for love to flourish in the midst of chaos. The city has grown from a humble trading post on the coast to a sprawling metropolis that is home to over 20 million people. Lagos has attracted migrants from across Nigeria and beyond, all drawn by the promise of work and a better life. They come with dreams of success, of mobility and of freedom, each one hoping to carve out a niche for themselves in this frenetic, forever-moving urban jungle. Lagos is often described as the commercial hub of Nigeria, the nerve-center of its economy, but for those who live here, the city is more than just a business hub. It's a place of endless possibility, of endless hustle. It's the spirit of Lagos that propels the city forward, a city that is driven by the people who inhabit it.

In a passionate and scathing critique delivered from the White House, President Barack Obama yesterday condemned a group of Senate Republicans who he claimed had chosen special interests over the American people by blocking a bipartisan plan to expand background checks on firearms. Speaking to our newspaper, Redknapp highlighted a worrying trend among England's emerging talents, suggesting that too many of them are suffering from groupthink and a sense of overconfidence, rather than the humility that comes with being part of the underdog nation. "The potential is there, but I think some of these young players think they've made it," Redknapp said candidly. "You need to be playing regular football, league football, not just a couple of games here and there. In Europe, the bank faces multiple investigations into its activities in the lead-up to the financial crisis, and it has been forced to write down significant amounts of debt in relation to the scandal. In total, Deutsche Bank has incurred losses in excess of €50bn (£43.5bn) in relation to the crisis, making it one of the biggest financial casualties of the past decade. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has announced that an investigation will be launched into claims that British soldiers abused Iraqi detainees during the 2003 invasion. Jails in crisis: a call for military intervention Sir David Ramsbotham, a former prison governor with over 40 years' experience, has spoken out about the dire state of Britain's prisons, warning that the government should consider calling in the Army to restore order in some facilities. His comments, made in an exclusive interview, highlight the extreme measures needed to address the systemic issues plaguing the UK's penal system. With record numbers of inmates on the verge of expulsion due to overcrowding, and staffing shortages causing chaos behind bars, Sir David's testimony paints a picture of institutions on the brink of collapse. The former governor, who served in some of the country's most notorious prisons, including Belmarsh and Parkhurst, is adamant that drastic action is required to tackle the crisis. "I have never seen things as bad as they are now," he told our correspondent. "Inmates are being attacked, staff are being attacked, and the infrastructure of the prisons is crumbling. It's a ticking time bomb, and unless something is done NOW, it will lead to catastrophic consequences." Sir David's solution may seem extreme, but he believes that the Army should be deployed to take control of those prisons deemed "not fit for purpose". He points to the success of the military's involvement in Northern Ireland's Maze Prison, where soldiers helped to restore order and reduce violence in the 1990s. "It's not a perfect solution, but it's one thing that might help to restore order and give us some breathing space," he said. The government has responded by committing additional funding to tackle the prisons' crisis, but Sir David remains skeptical. "The problem is that the government is trying to deal with symptoms rather than addressing the root causes," he said. "Prisons are not just about punishment; they're about reform and rehabilitation. We need to rethink our entire approach to corrections, and that means investing in education, training, and support for inmates." As we visited some of the country's most troubled prisons, the reality of the crisis became all too apparent. Overcrowding, conflicts between rival gangs, and staff shortages have created a perfect storm of unrest. Inmates are living in squalor, with reported cases of poor hygiene, inadequate nutrition, and a lack of access to basic facilities. Sir David's plea for military intervention has sparked debate among prison reformers and politicians, with some questioning whether the Army has the necessary skills and expertise to tackle the complex issues behind prisons.

Scottish Economy Woes Escalate: Business Surveys Paint Bleak Picture Scotland's economic prospects are beginning to look increasingly bleak, according to two separate business surveys that have prompted concerns about the country's prolonged economic downturn. The impact of Brexit, a resilient pound, and dwindling consumer confidence have all taken their toll on Scotland's economy, with some experts warning that the country may be on the cusp of a more severe recession. The latest survey from the Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) paint a dire picture, with 63% of companies reporting a decrease in profits over the past three months. This is up from 44% in the previous quarter, and is the largest quarterly increase in profit decline since 2009, when the UK was plagued by the global financial crisis. The survey also found that confidence among Scottish businesses is at a record low, with 73% of respondents citing factors such as Brexit uncertainty, the Scottish Government's flagging policies, and international markets as influencing their decision-making. Moreover, 69% of companies reported a fall in orders, with 34% citing a significant decline - a stark indication of the current economic stagnation. Meanwhile, the Scottish Building Federation's (SBF) quarterly business monitor revealed a similar tale of woe, with 73% of its member companies experiencing a decline in activity over the past quarter. The SBF attributed this decline to a perfect storm of factors, including the client pipeline shrinking, uncertain economic forecasts, and changes to government policies. According to Ishbel Gosse, Chief Executive of the SBF, the figures are a 'stark reminder' of the scale of the economic challenge Scotland faces. "Construction is a key driver of Scotland's economy, and these results suggest that the sector is struggling to cope with the uncertainty surrounding Brexit," she warned. David Harker, regional executive for Scotland at the RBS, echoed these concerns, stating that the business confidence index has sunk to its lowest level since the RBS began tracking the data in 2002. "The current economic conditions are creating a great deal of uncertainty for businesses, which is limiting their ability to invest and grow," he noted. Amid these signs of economic distress, the Scottish Government is under increasing pressure to introduce more supportive policies to catalyze economic growth and reverse this decline. However, the May election, plus increased contention within the Scottish and British governments, means the plans for government intervention on this matter are at present unclear.

Jimmy Carter, the 39th President of the United States, has long been an outspoken advocate for combating devastating tropical diseases that have plagued millions of people worldwide for far too long. Now, he is leading a bold initiative that he believes will bring about a historic breakthrough in the fight against Guinea worm disease, a parasitic infection that has been the subject of his tireless efforts over the past few decades. Mr Carter, who served as President from 1977 to 1981 and has dedicated a considerable amount of time to humanitarian work since leaving office, has compared the push to eradicate Guinea worm disease to the successful campaigns to wipe out smallpox, which was ultimately eliminated from the world in 1980. The Carter Centre, which is spearheading the Guinea worm eradication effort, recently announced that the number of reported cases of the disease had fallen by nearly 99% since its peak in the mid-1980s. Guinea worm disease is a waterborne parasite that is spread through contaminated water and typically affects people in poor and rural areas. When a person drinks water infected with the parasite, it causes extreme pain, discomfort, and inflammation that can ultimately lead to the fatal extraction of the worm from the skin. According to the Carter Centre, there were just 28 reported cases of Guinea worm disease last year, down from over 3.5 million cases in 1986, the year Mr Carter first became involved in the eradication campaign. The former President is now confident that his team will be able to mark Guinea worm disease as the second successful eradication of a human parasite in history, following smallpox. "We're doing all right," Mr Carter said in a statement earlier this month. "If we can continue the progress we've made and get the remaining cases down to zero, I think we can achieve eradication in the next three years." This ambitious goal will depend on the continued dedication and support of governments, communities, and health workers around the world who have played a critical role in the fight against Guinea worm disease. Mr Carter said the final push will require "a lot of effort" and that his team would need to continue to work closely with affected areas, governments, and other partners to find every single case of the disease and eradicate it. Guineaworm Eradication Programme director and Carter Centre Vice President Dr Donald Hopkins, who has led the effort alongside Mr Carter, expressed similar optimism about the prospects for Guinea worm disease eradication, saying: "I have every confidence that together through this joint international effort, we can eradicate this devastating disease."

The Compassionate Conversation: The Inspiring Legacy of Dr Kate Granger Five years ago, Dr Kate Granger's life was turned upside down when she received a diagnosis of cancer that would ultimately claim her life. But instead of letting the news define her, Kate harnessed her experience to make a profound impact on the way hospitals communicate with patients. As she herself suffered through the challenges of diagnosis, treatment, and recovery, Kate became convinced that something was fundamentally wrong with the way medical staff spoke to patients and their families. "I was diagnosed with a very rare and aggressive form of cancer, and I soon discovered that the hospital staff hadn't received specialist training in how to break bad news," she once said. "My own experience was soul-destroying, and I knew that I wanted to do something to prevent similar suffering for other patients and their families." Thus began Kate's remarkable journey, as she set out to change the face of doctor-patient relations and establish a new standard for compassionate care. In 2011, Kate launched the #HelloMyNameIs campaign, a rallying cry for healthcare professionals to introduce themselves to patients and talk to them in a way that was clear, relevant, and respectful. Almost overnight, the initiative took off, as hospitals, medical schools, and healthcare organisations across the UK and beyond adopted Kate's simple yet powerful message. But Dr Granger's legacy extends far beyond the impressive reach of her campaign. In her final years, she also founded the 'Time to Listen' charity, which aimed to provide end-of-life training for medical staff and help hospitals build stronger, more supportive relationships with patients and their families. In just five short years, the charity raised an astonishing £656,000, almost exclusively through donations from the public. Kate's fundraising efforts were always driven by a deep empathy for others and a determination to put patients at the heart of everything the healthcare system did. And despite her own frailty, she consistently demonstrated an incredible energy and generosity of spirit, inspiring countless people with her courage, humour, and compassion. Dr Granger's passing has left a huge void, but her work lives on. In a world where illness and hardship can all too often feel overwhelming, Kate Granger showed us that even in the darkest moments, there is always the chance to make a difference and to leave behind a lasting legacy of love, kindness, and care.

Embracing Emotion: Why Fearing to Feel Can Lead to Decreased Happiness Research has long shown that the way we perceive and experience emotions plays a crucial role in determining our overall well-being. While many of us strive for happiness and try to avoid negative emotions like anger and hatred, a groundbreaking new study suggests that suppressing these feelings can actually have the opposite effect, leading to a decrease in happiness. The study, conducted by a team of researchers at University College London (UCL), questioned whether avoiding unpleasant emotions can indeed contribute to feelings of unhappiness. According to the study, published in the journal Psychological Science, individuals are happier when they are able to feel the emotions they desire, even if those emotions are unpleasant. "Emotions serve an important motivational function," said Dr Mark Solms, the lead author of the study. "They drive us to act and communicate, to have social interactions, and to pursue our goals." However, Dr Solms emphasised, bottling up these emotions can "impede emotional functioning and well-being." To better understand the relationship between emotion expression, suppression, and happiness, researchers examined the experiences of more than 3,000 individuals across the United States and the UK. Participants were asked to rate the intensity of various emotions, including positive emotions like happiness and love, and negative emotions like anger, hatred, and sadness. Results yielded a surprising finding: those who were able to express their emotions, both positive and negative, reported higher levels of happiness. This suggests that the feelings we often try to suppress - such as anger and hatred - serve a vital purpose, such as alerting us to potential threats or driving us to take action to assert our boundaries. In essence, the study's findings indicate that rather than striving to bottle up and suppress emotions, we should instead attempt to develop an open and accepting mindset towards our feelings. This means acknowledging and accepting - even embracing - our full range of emotions, including those that we might typically view as negative. According to Dr Solms, by adopting this mindset, we can actually create more space within ourselves for positive emotions to flourish. "When we are open to experiencing a wide range of emotions, we are more likely to feel emotional fluidity," he explained, suggesting that this increased emotional flexibility can enable us to navigate the ups and downs of life with greater ease. Ultimately, the study's findings offer a compelling case for the importance of emotional acceptance - including the existence of unpleasant emotions - in achieving high levels of happiness.

Liberal Democrat Minister Calls for Teachers to be Paid Fairly, Amid Growing Recruitment Crisis Teachers should be compensated fairly for their hard work and dedication, according to Liberal Democrat Schools Minister David Laws. In a bold statement, Mr Laws has emphasized the need to value teachers through their pay packets, as concerns continue to grow over the UK's teacher recruitment crisis. The Government has been under increasing pressure to address the alarming rates of teacher resignation and low morale in the profession. Figures show that nearly 60,000 teachers have left the classroom since 2010, with many citing poor pay and conditions as a major factor in their decision to quit. "We need to value teachers through their pay packet," Mr Laws said in an interview. "Teachers have a critical role to play in shaping the minds of future generations and we must recognize that by paying them a salary that reflects their hard work and dedication." Mr Laws' comments come as the Liberal Democrats push for the Government to increase teachers' pay to a level that is more in line with other professionals with similar qualifications. "Teachers are in short supply and demand for places is at an all-time high," he said. "We can't afford to lose any more talented and committed individuals from the profession." The call for teacher pay reform has been met with approval from teaching unions, who have long highlighted the need for increased funding for the profession. "We welcome David Laws' recognition of the need to value teachers through their pay," said National Association of Schoolmasters Union of Women Teachers (NASUWT) general secretary Chris Keates. "It is high time the Government took a more realistic view of the value of teachers to our society and increased funding to ensure that we can recruit and retain the best possible staff for our schools." However, others have expressed skepticism about Mr Laws' claims, citing the limitations of pay alone as a solution to the recruitment crisis. "While pay is certainly an important factor, it is not the only consideration for teachers," said Anthony Seldon, a leading education expert and Master of Wellington College. "Teachers are also motivated by a desire to make a positive impact on their students' lives and to work in an environment that supports their own professional development." The debate over teacher pay is set to continue as the Liberal Democrats push for more funding for the profession.

The 14th Conference of the Parties (COP14) of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) has got underway in the city of Sharm El-Sheikh's sister city, Ekurhuleni, located on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's economic hub. Some 10,000 people from around the globe gathered at the convention - known as the 'Earth's largest biodiversity conference' - to tackle the alarming decline of species on our planet. The talks come as a report released by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) earlier this month revealed that over 450 species are now at risk of extinction, while the global wildlife population has declined by an average of 60% since 1970. This includes the massive African elephant, which has seen its numbers drop dramatically in recent years due to poaching and habitat loss. The IUCN report found that only around 415,000 African elephants remain in the wild, down from 700,000 just a decade ago. Conservationists are pressing governments to take concrete action to protect the majestic creatures and their habitats, but divisions remain over issues such as the culling of elephants for conservation purposes. "It's a war against species, and humans are the enemy," Dr Tom Lovejoy, a world-renowned conservationist, told the gathering. "We can no longer just protect species in isolation; we need to link conservation with development. The focus must shift from just conserving species to ensuring the long-term sustainability of human societies." African elephant poaching has been extremely high in some countries, driven by the demand for ivory in Asia. The standing chairman of the Botswana Elephant Productivity Board, Percy Tumba, told the conference that almost 150 tonnes of ivory - enough to be sold in Europe - had been seized in the past five years in Botswana alone. Botswana currently plans to give its 130,000 elephants their own "carnivore colonies". Tumba pointed out that increased poaching would strain the ecosystem to the point, where for the sake of the environment as well as human safety, elephants and other resident carnivores would have no chance against each other. He pressed the development of technologies that aid 'cowboys and cowgirls' in caring for the herds, plus assure that the additional revenue wildlife tourism provides the animals is kept in reserve - alongside other funds - until habitat conditions improve. Tragedy Struck the Hajj Pilgrimage: Investigation Launched into Mecca Crane Collapse The esteemed city of Mecca, a place of profound spiritual and historical significance to Muslims around the world, has been marred by an unthinkable tragedy. A crane, which was operated by Saudi Binladin Group, a major construction company in Saudi Arabia, collapsed on Friday at around 6:00 pm local time. The devastating incident occurred at the Abraj Al-Bait Clock Tower in the heart of the holy city, a location thought to be a safe area, just hours before the Eid al-Adha holiday and at the peak of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Eyewitnesses described the horrific scene, where scores of people were crushed or trapped beneath the wreckage, with some reporting hearing terrified screams and seeing an ensuing stampede. Emergency services rushed to the scene but, alas, the damage had been done, and the death toll keeps rising. According to official reports, a total of 107 people have lost their lives so far, while over 200 were injured in the calamitous event. On Saturday, Saudi Arabia's King Salman went onto the airwaves, addressing the nation after the disaster, describing it as a "terrible" event. He expressed his deepest condolences to the victims and their families, promising a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crane's collapse. Conceding that this was a "calamity" that would be probed with the utmost urgency, the monarch vowed to identify those responsible and ensure that the damages are compensated. Saudi authorities have formally launched an investigation, which was overseen by the Minister of Commerce and Industry, Majid bin Abdullah Al-Qassabi. The authorities are looking into the construction process that led to the crane being installed in the first place, as well as statements from witnesses gathered on scene. They sought to clarify whether the crane was the sole cause of the disaster and determine whether neglect or some form of human error were contributing factors. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al-Moshari, the head of the Civil Defence in the holy region, told the Al Ekhbariya TV that the crane, which was operated by a foreign worker, had crashed down from a height of 30 meters. He identified 30 countries whose citizens were among the dead and injured victims of the incident, highlighting how the international community has a great stake in returning to a brighter period of pilgrimage in Makkah. Diplomats from countries impacted have been informed about the status of their citizens who took part in the pilgrimage.

Jamil Daniels, a 31-year-old former officer with the Milwaukee Police Department, was charged on Tuesday with first-degree reckless homicide in connection with the shooting of Joel Acevedo on August 7. Acevedo, a 29-year-old man, was unarmed when Daniels allegedly shot him in the head while he was asleep at an apartment in Milwaukee. According to prosecutors, Daniels had gone to the apartment with another officer to investigate a domestic dispute. Once inside, a physical altercation broke out between Daniels and Acevedo, who was sleeping in a bedroom. The other officer attempted to break up the fight, but ultimately remained at the scene while Daniels left the room. Moments later, the sound of a gunshot was heard coming from the bedroom, and the other officer reportedly discovered Acevedo lying on the floor, bleeding from a head wound. Acevedo died shortly after being taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead due to the gunshot wound to the head, according to the Milwaukee County Medical Examiner's Office. Initially, Milwaukee Police Department had claimed that Acevedo had exhibited aggressive behaviour and had been threatening Daniels before the shooting. However, the charges filed by prosecutors suggest that those accounts were inaccurate, and that Acevedo was entirely unarmed when shot. "The evidence does not support the initial accounts provided by the police department," said Milwaukee County District Attorney John Chisholm. "Mr. Acevedo was a victim of a reckless and unlawful shooting by Mr. Daniels." Daniels, who left the police department in 2014, has been in custody since August 22, when he was originally charged with second-degree reckless endangerment. The new charge of first-degree reckless homicide carries a maximum sentence of up to 60 years in prison. Representative and civil rights groups across Milwaukee have expressed outrage over the incident, calling for transparency and justice for the Acevedo family. Coroner's inquest opens into Lindt cafe siege A harrowing chapter in Australia's history is set to be re-examined as a coroner's inquest opened into the Lindt cafe siege in Sydney, which left two innocent hostages and a gunman dead in 2014. On the morning of 15 December that year, group of hostages were taken captive at the Chart House cafe in Martin Place, which is directly opposite the iconic Sydney Opera House. A lone gunman, Man Haron Monis, a 49-year-old Iranian-born Iranian-French dual national, demanded to speak to the Australian prime minister and made a series of chilling threats. The deeply disturbing 16-hour standoff eventually came to a violent end on the evening of 16 December, when Monis took the lives of two of the hostages, Tori Johnson and Katrina Dawson, before NSW Police tactical officers stormed the premises, bringing the tragedy to an end. Inquests into the siege were initially delayed, with the New South Wales coroner announcing an inquiry would be held "as soon as practicable" in February 2015. Almost nine years on, the inquest finally got underway, with Coroner Teresa O'Sullivan, who conducted the inquest into the 2019 Tomlinson's toque factory and mezzanine floor collapse in Western Sydney, hearing evidence from investigators and witnesses. "In this inquest... I will have regard to: (a) the circumstances, cause and circumstances of the deaths of all persons deceased during this incident, (b) any other matters brought to the attention of the inquest by the inquiring officer," Coroner O'Sullivan said in a statement earlier this week. In June 2020, almost six years after the inquest's proposed commencement, Detective Wayne Schipper, the commander of the Police Media and Welfare unit at the time of the siege, revealed the investigation into the 2014 atrocity was ongoing. Assistant commissioner Malcolm Linton said the investigation had become one of Australia's most complex, with hundreds of investigations running concurrently. The lengthy inquiry sought to examine all the facets surrounding the events of that fateful day, including the actions of Monis, the involvement of law enforcement and the measures taken by the café operators to protect their patrons. On the eve of the inquest this week the family of Tori Johnson, one of those whose lives were claimed by Monis, said in a statement: "In every passing year, the wounds of this day remain open and painful, though they are healing.

Children online are increasingly at risk of being targeted by sex offenders, the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) has sounded the alarm. The charity has launched a new campaign to educate young people on how to stay safe online and to warn parents and guardians about the dangers of the internet. The NSPCC group children's charity has highlighted the ease with which sex offenders can use the internet to groom and exploit children. "The internet can be a playground for paedophiles," said a spokesperson for the charity. "They can sit in the comfort of their own homes and use the internet to contact and manipulate children, often under the guise of friendship." In the past year, the NSPCC has received over 10,000 calls to its helpline from children who have been contacted by someone online. The most common type of abuse by far is grooming, where the offender builds a relationship with the child before meeting up with them in person. According to the NSPCC, sex offenders are using social media sites, online games and chat rooms to target children. They often use fake profiles and pretend to be the same age as their victims. "It's easy for children to trust someone who is pretending to be like them," said Tom Keatinge, a NSPCC child protection expert. "Children need to be aware of the dangers of online relationships and the importance of keeping their private life private." The NSPCC is urging parents and guardians to have open and honest conversations with their children about online safety and to set boundaries and rules for their online activities. Children also need to be aware of the following online safety tips:   Never talk to a stranger online   Never meet someone you have met online in person   Don't share pictures or personal details with strangers online   Tell an adult if someone is sending you messages that make you feel uncomfortable The NSPCC is calling on social media companies to do more to protect children from abuse and exploitation online. They are also urging parents to report any suspicious activity to the police. For those who have been affected, the NSPCC has a 24-hour helpline number, 0808 800 5000. As a society, we need to do more to protect our children from harm. By working together, we can make the internet a safer place for all children.

Councils across England face a "perfect storm" due to a catastrophic rise in adult social care costs, with many warning that they will not be able to cope with the growing burden without substantial investment. The sharp increase in care costs, largely driven by a surge in demand due to an ageing population and the impact of years of austerity, is being exacerbated by inflation and a lack of funding, say local authorities. And despite planned council tax rises, these will do little to alleviate the crisis, as officials warn they are unlikely to be enough to cover the projected costs. The demand for care services is rising sharply, with older adults and disabled people increasingly in need of support. This is having a devastating impact on finances, with one in six councils facing a statutory review because they are struggling to meet the adult social care elements of their duties, according to the Local Government Association (LGA). Barry Singleton, who chairs Bexley Council's Adult Services Committee, said that authorities were facing a "credibility crisis". "We've been talking about this for years, but nothing has been done to address the underlying problems," he said, citing spiralling demand and a lack of resources. "Walking down the high street, you see heavy hearted faces everywhere. I see elderly people who have been to see their doctor and have been told, 'I've got to go home, I need a care package'. It breaks my heart." LGA chair James Jamieson called for urgent action to address the dire situation, which he said had been exacerbated by the triple whammy of rising demand, inflation and the scrapping of government ring-fenced funding. The government has planned a 3% council tax increase across England, which will generate almost £1 billion by 2025. However, this is seen as insufficient to address the projected costs of adult social care. Local government leaders point out that the cost of elderly care is rising sharply because of rising care home costs, an increase in people needing high-level support, and strain on acute hospital services. To bridge the gap, councils are being forced to cut services, delay support and raise more through the precept on council tax, adding to burdens on cash-strapped householders. James Jamieson said that while councils had managed to find savings and eradicate unnecessary bureaucracy, more drastic action was needed to ensure local-area services could continue.

Iraqi forces launched a long-awaited assault on the Old City, the last stronghold of so-called Islamic State in Mosul, on Sunday, but their advance was met with fierce resistance from the group's fighters. The offensive began at dawn, with Iraqi troops supported by US-led coalition airstrikes and artillery fire moving into the densely populated neighborhood. But as the group's fighters - known as Isis - held their ground, coalition aircraft launched repeated strikes to try and clear a path for the Iraqi troops. A total of 50 Isis fighters were killed by airstrikes on Sunday, but the area is heavily populated with civilians and there are concerns about the use of heavy explosives in such a densely populated area. "It's very, very difficult," said one Iraqi soldier. "There are many buildings, narrow streets. The Isis fighters have rigged many parts of the city with explosives and that's a big challenge for us." Estimates suggest that tens of thousands of civilians are trapped in the Old City, which is packed tightly with buildings and narrow alleys, and coalition officials worry that a landmine or IED could explode at any moment and devastate the area. "It's not just the Isis fighters we have to worry about," explained General Gary Volesky, the commander of coalition ground forces in Iraq. "We have to be worried about the explosive-laden booby traps laid by Isis. We've seen that in other parts of Mosul. We're working hard to mitigate that risk, but it's a tough challenge." The offensive is being led by the Golden Division, an elite unit of Iraqi troops who have been instrumental in the recapture of large parts of Mosul in recent weeks. They are supported by a group of clan fighters who are well-versed in the narrow streets and alleys of the Old City. "The battle is extremely intense," said one commander in the Golden Division. "As we enter the city, we see that the Isis fighters have booby-trapped most of the areas we're moving through. We have to clear the buildings, but first we must be careful. There are also Isis snipers in the buildings who are firing on our soldiers." The failure to take control of the Old City quickly could lead to a protracted and bloody campaign, with the potential for hundreds of civilian casualties. "The battle for the Old City will be a brutal and difficult fight," said the Iraqi Prime Minister, Haider al-Abadi, who visited the front lines on Sunday.

The prospect of Britain leaving the European Union is a complex one, with many questions still hanging in the balance. One of the most pressing concerns for many is what an exit could mean for trade and the economy. We've been inundated with emails, tweets and letters from listeners sharing their thoughts and concerns, and we've asked some of the UK's leading experts in trade and economics to help us make sense of the situation. For many, the idea of " Brexit" conjures up visions of a chaotic and unstable trade environment, with imports and exports grinding to a halt. However, others are more optimistic, arguing that the UK's decision to leave the EU could ultimately prove to be aBrexit opportunity, allowing Britain to forge its own trade deals and sidestep the red tape of EU regulations. The most obvious question is what will happen to Britain's current trade arrangements with the EU. At the moment, the country is part of the EU's single market, which allows goods and services to move freely between member states. However, if the UK leaves the EU, it will automatically cease to be part of the single market, and trade barriers could arise. The Institute of Directors, a leading business lobby group, has warned that an exit from the EU could see Britain's businesses facing tariffs and quotas on goods they export to the EU, potentially putting thousands of jobs at risk. However, others argue that this could be a golden opportunity for Britain to renegotiate its trade deals with the EU and to pursue new agreements with other countries. The UK's trade secretary, Liam Fox, has argued that an exit from the EU could see Britain gaining access to new markets in countries such as China and the US, which currently restrict access to the EU's single market. He also argued that Britain could be a leader in the advocacy of free trade, given its tradition of being an offshore financial centre. Dr Patrick Minford, an economics professor at Cardiff University, agrees that the UK is well-placed to take advantage of new trade opportunities outside the EU. He argues that the UK has "a unique advantage" when it comes to negotiating trade deals, thanks to its unique relationships with countries like the US, Japan and Australia. "The UK can be a leader in trade negotiations and can participate in the development of global trade agreements," he says.

The sleepless dreams of corporate success: is it time to wake up to a better way to work? The esteemed boardrooms of the financial world, though it may seem counterintuitive, have long prided themselves ontheir employees' ability to sacrifice sleep for the sake of work. For years, the less you slept, the more dedicated and driven you were - or so the narrative went. One leading executive who agrees with the notion of prioritising sleep is Nigel Risner, business growth strategist and an expert in leadership psychology. It seems, then, that the notion of sacrificing sleep for the sake of corporate success may be eroding. Increasingly, companies like Amazon, Nike and Microsoft are embracing sleep-friendly practices, which give employees greater autonomy to recharge. Kate Lister, CEO of the World Sleep Day Organisation, champions this shift.

The Home Affairs Select Committee (HASC) has made the recommendation after investigating the current formula, which is widely seen as unfair and in need of reform. MPs on the committee, chaired by Yvette Cooper, concluded that the current system, which distributes policing funding to 43 forces in England and Wales, is too complex and favours more affluent areas with higher population levels. Under the existing formula, officers in some areas benefit from additional funding due to higher "deprivation scores", which account for socioeconomic factors such as crime rates and unemployment. At the same time, it was heard how others are finding themselves without the proper budget for data room gear in many of the police stations they are being posted to. As an example one police inspector from a small rural force told the committee that their area's deprivation factor was artificially low, despite having high levels of poverty and deprivation. This means that the force receives less government funding, making it harder to provide the same level of service as larger, more affluent areas. The weekly, which has been told by officials that some police forces in England and Wales have lost out on hundreds of millions of pounds under the existing formula, welcomed the committee's recommendation. "A new funding formula must be fair, transparent and based on current needs," Tom Winsor, the former HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary, told our reporter. Home Secretary Amber Rudd has said that she would review the current funding formula after reviewing police funding overall, and that police chiefs had told her that the existing system was "unsustainable". Despite the long-standing problems with the existing formula, the Home Office has shown little signs of tackling the issue in recent years. The MP-led group made the argument that the roots of the debacle that almost every police department that had asked for help be tagged with a real reason going back in time. Barry Sheerman MP, a Labour member of the committee, concluded the investigation, praising the contribution of "courageous" whistleblowers who came forward with "stark" evidence of the formula's flaws. Sheersman said the "tentacles of neglect" from certain grandfathered motions that have trickled down from more then 26 years ago need to be dealt with bringing radical change. It now remains to be seen how the government will respond to the committee's recommendation. With a new funding formula potentially worth hundreds of millions of pounds, there is a great deal at stake.

In an age of digital disruption and fragmentation, where traditional notions of journalism and media consumption are being continually challenged, the question of what constitutes the most important and powerful source of news is more complex than ever. With the rise of social media giants, online news aggregators, and citizen journalists, the landscape has become increasingly crowded and noisy. However, despite this shifting landscape, one organisation continues to stand out as a beacon of authority and influence - the BBC. Founded in 1922, the British Broadcasting Corporation has grown to become a global institution, synonymous with unbiased, impartial, and high-quality news and current affairs programming. The BBC's global reach is staggering, with an estimated 379 million people watching or using its services every week. Its editorial values of accuracy, depth, and fairness are respected and emulated by journalists around the world. The organisation's commitment to fact-based reporting, its investigative journalism, and its willingness to hold those in power to account have solidified its reputation as a trusted source of information. Moreover, the BBC's influence extends far beyond its global audience. It shapes international news agendas, influences public opinion, and informs policymakers. The organisation's flagship current affairs programmes, such as the Today programme, Newsnight, and Panorama, are widely regarded as the gold standard of journalism, and are closely followed by politicians, business leaders, and other influencers. While social media platforms and online news aggregators may have disrupted traditional viewing habits and fragmented audiences, the BBC's enduring appeal lies in its ability to deliver in-depth, nuanced, and well-researched reporting that informs and illuminates. Its global reach, journalistic excellence, and editorial integrity make it the most important source of news and the most powerful media organisation in the world today. However, some media analysts and experts argue that the rise of online platforms, particularly Google and Facebook, have transformed the way we consume news and have become the most powerful media players. These organisations determine which news stories get seen and heard, and their algorithms and advertising models have a profound impact on the types of content that are produced and disseminated. Other contenders for the most powerful media organisation in the world include The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and Al Jazeera, each with its own unique strengths and global reach. However, the BBC's dominant position, its reach, and its impact on the global information landscape make a strong case for it as the most important and powerful source of news today.

Senior Police Officer Allowed to Retire Amid Ongoing Investigation In a highly unusual move, a senior Metropolitan Police officer involved in a high-profile operation in which a man was shot dead by police is being allowed to retire, despite being under investigation. The decision has sparked widespread concern among civil liberties groups and the family of the victim, who are calling for greater transparency and accountability. The operation, which took place in January last year, resulted in the death of Kingsley Burrell, a 29-year-old mental health patient who was being restrained by police. The incident was heavily criticized by the family and local community, who expressed concerns that excessive force had been used. The senior officer, who has not been named, is accused of misleading a coroner and failing to disclose crucial information about the events leading up to Mr. Burrell's death. An internal police investigation by the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards found "serious misconduct" by the officer, including "deception and concealment" about the circumstances of the shooting. However, in a surprise move, the officer has been allowed to retire, citing "health reasons". The decision has been met with outrage by campaigners and the Independent Police Complaints Commission, who have called for a fuller inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Mr. Burrell's death. The IPCC said it was "deeply disappointed" by the Met's decision, stating that it is "extremely difficult to understand" why the officer was allowed to retire without being subject to the full rigour of the inquiry process. "The investigation into the death of Kingsley Burrell remains ongoing, and we would have expected the officer in question to have been suspended from duty pending its outcome," a spokesperson said. The family of Kingsley Burrell have also expressed their dismay at the news, calling for "total transparency and accountability" over the events leading up to their loved one's death. "We demand to know why the officer involved has been allowed to retire and why the Met is protecting them," said a statement from the Burrell family. "Our son did not deserve to die in the way that he did. We will continue to fight for the truth and for justice." The Metropolitan Police Service has been under growing pressure in recent months to increase transparency and accountability, particularly in high-profile incidents involving police use of force. The decision to allow the senior officer to retire has only added to the pressure, with many calling for a thorough overhaul of the Met's disciplinary procedures.

The eternal debate surrounding tennis and the Olympics continues to cause a stir amongst sports enthusiasts. On one hand, it seems remarkable that a sport that has produced some of the world's most lavish events, including Wimbledon, remains a staple of the Olympic Games. The grandeur and prestige that comes with competing in the Olympics is undeniable, and it is little wonder that the world's top tennis players clamour to take part. However, as pointed out by critics, the values of a multimillion-pound sport like tennis somewhat contravene the spirit of amateurism that has historically defined the Olympics. The financial rewards available to professional tennis players are staggering, with the likes of Roger Federer and Serena Williams commanding prize money of millions of pounds for their services. Meanwhile, the costs associated with staging the Olympics have become increasingly eye-watering, with billions of pounds being ploughed into facilities and infrastructure to accommodate the influx of top athletes. At the same time, there can be no disputing the desire of the world's top players to participate in the Olympics. The likes of Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal and Andy Murray, to name just a few, have all spoken of the enormous enjoyment they derive from competing at the highest level against their peers. And while there may be a degree of financial gain to be made, it is not the primary motivator for these elite athletes. As former world number one Andy Murray recently pointed out, representing one's country at the Olympics is an unparalleled honour, providing the opportunity to connect with a global audience and inspire a new generation of tennis fans. As the Olympic qualification process is set in motion, it will be fascinating to observe which players are prepared to leap into the unknown and dedicate themselves to the pursuit of an Olympic medal. Will Rafael Nadal's swashbuckling flair in front of a partisan crowd be enough to propel him to the gold medal podium in the singles competition? Or will Novak Djokovic's consummate professionalism and court craftsman-like abilities see him navigate the unforgiving terrain of the doubles tournament and claim the spoils? Whatever the outcome, one thing is for certain: the tennis competition at the Olympics will throw up its fair share of intriguing storylines, electrifying moments and tense showdowns. As the world's top players gather in Tokyo to compete on the biggest stage in sport, the Olympic spirit will be very much alive and pulsating throughout every frame of the action.

Outdoor advertising is a ubiquitous presence on city streets around the world, plastering advertisements for everything from fast food to cars to smartphones. But not Jordan Seiler. Seiler, a Brooklyn-based artist and anti-advertising activist, has made it his mission to take down as many of these ads as he can. For years, he has been quietly dismantling billboards and blight-causing advertisements in urban areas, posting them on social media and using the hashtag #leaveconsidertheoptions. And it's not just the ads themselves that Seiler objects to, but the way they warp our perception of public space and the kinds of data that are being collected about us every time we walk down the street. Seiler's frustration with outdoor advertising is rooted in the way it dominates public spaces, often obscuring the beauty and history of the built environment with plastic and steel. "I just think that the proliferation of billboards is really an absurdity," he said in an interview. "They're just a waste. Fertility charity, I Wish, has written to Scottish Health Secretary, Jeane Freeman, to advocate for the expansion of IVF (In Vitro Fertilization) services for couples struggling to conceive. Today marks a pivotal moment in the history of our nation as the UK begins to decide its future in the European Union. For nearly five decades, our country has been a member of the EU, with all the benefits and challenges that come with it. Now, after years of debate and controversy, the British people have been given the chance to have their say in a historic referendum that will determine the course of our nation's path forward. As the polls open at 7am this morning, voters across the country will be making their way to the ballot box to cast their vote in the "Stay" or "Leave" camp. The outcome of this referendum will have far-reaching consequences for our economy, our politics, and our society. It is a decision that will be shaped by a complex array of factors, from the economic benefits of free trade with our European partners to the desire for greater control over our own borders and laws. At the heart of this debate lies a question about the relationship between the UK and its European neighbours. Should we remain a part of a unified Europe, working together to address the challenges of the 21st century? Or should we strike out on our own, charting a new course for a Britain that is free to pursue its own destiny, unencumbered by the constraints of EU membership? Throughout this campaign, both sides have presented their arguments with passion and conviction. The "Remain" camp has pointed to the economic benefits of EU membership, from access to a vast single market of over 500 million people to the free movement of workers and goods. They have also highlighted the importance of European cooperation on issues such as climate change, counter-terrorism, and international development. In contrast, the "Leave" camp has emphasized the desire for greater control over our own affairs, from the shape of our immigration policy to the size of our fishing quotas. They have also raised concerns about the impact of EU membership on our national sovereignty and the ability of our politicians to make decisions in our best interests. As the votes are cast, one thing is clear: the outcome of this referendum will be a major shock to the system. Whether or not the UK remains a part of the EU, this decision will have far-reaching implications for our politics, our economy, and our society.

A team of researchers at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics has made a major breakthrough in the search for life beyond Earth. In a study published on Monday, the scientists revealed that they have successfully detected an atmosphere around a planet that is eerily similar to our own. The exoplanet, known as K2-18b, is a super-Earth located about 111 light-years from the Sun in the constellation Leo. Researchers say that signs of an atmosphere on K2-18b were previously detected in 2015, but new data has now confirmed the presence of a gaseous layer surrounding the planet. According to Dr Sarah Blunt, lead author of the study, the team used observations from NASA's Kepler space telescope to detect the atmospheric signature of K2-18b. "We have an incredible dataset from Kepler with more than eight years of observations, and we knew that if there was an atmosphere on K2-18b, we should be able to see it," Dr Blunt said in a statement. K2-18b is considered a prime target for the search for life beyond Earth due to its size and temperature. The planet is roughly two times bigger than Earth, and orbits its star at a distance similar to our own star's. Scientists were astonished to discover that K2-18b is surrounded by a dense atmosphere, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium. Researchers speculate that the atmosphere may be maintained by a strong geothermal radiation from the planet's internal heat, which could imply that K2-18b may have a solid surface and a liquid water content, similar to Earth. "This is the first time we've detected a clear sign of atmosphere around a super-Earth like K2-18b," said Dr Johanna Teske, a research scientist at the Carnegie Institution for Science, who was not involved in the study but praised the findings. "The detection of atmosphere on K2-18b has significant implications for the ongoing search for life beyond our solar system." The discovery has sent shockwaves through the scientific community, given the significance of K2-18b and the prospects of finding life beyond Earth. Historically, the search for life has mostly focused on planets with conditions that are thought to favour life. Now, scientists are one step closer to finding more exoplanets similar to Earth. "The fact that we've found an atmosphere on a planet with similar conditions to Earth is a significant step forward," said Dr Sara Seager, a professor of astrophysics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

In a surprise revelation, a newly-promoted health minister has expressed support for allowing individuals in the UK to obtain assistance to end their lives, provided they meet strict criteria and guidelines. The comments have sparked a heated debate on the contentious issue, with some critics accusing the minister of flip-flopping on the matter. Stepping into the midst of this sensitive issue, Ed Argar, who was promoted to the position of Under-Secretary of State at the Department of Health and Social Care, surprised many by declaring that those who are suffering from unbearable pain or terminal illness should be permitted to seek medical aid to end their lives. Speaking at a parliamentary debate, Mr Argar notably acknowledged the intricate complexities of assisted dying and expressed his understanding of the contrasting opinions on the matter. However, critics of the promotion of assisted dying argue that it opens the floodgates for vulnerable people, particularly the elderly and those with disabilities, to be pressured into ending their lives. They assert that introducing such legislation would put more pressure on relatives and social services to persuade individuals to opt for euthanasia. Leading the opposition is Palliative Aid, the leading UK-based palliative care society that is highly critical of those supporting the new bill. Those who are in favour of assisted dying claim that Mr Argar's comments are a welcome step, coming at a time when British citizens are ardently advocating for a more compassionate approach to end-of-life care. Proponents of the measure, such as organisations such as Dignity in Dying argue that this type of legislation will only work if patients are psychiatically fit and are able to make informed decisions. The Minister also pointed out the requirement of a stringent eligibility criteria that guarantees the individual meet the psychological and physical criteria to help avoid abuse and pressure and be protected from inducing potential suffering others. Twenty-five British people travelled to Switzerland last year to end their lives, a figure that the elderly campaigners have been steadfastly calling for action and claims reveal an increase from the previous year and feel is a strain on an economy. The division among politicians on the matter makes it impossible to know if any grandfathered motions will pass through the British parliament anytime soon. As debate rages, pro-choice advocates stress that individuals must have the right to self-determination if they are of sound mind to make this decision with no one forcing this unwanted option on them at all.

Sheffield Wednesday secured a crucial victory over second-placed Newcastle United last night, moving a step closer to qualifying for the Championship play-offs. The Owls, who are currently sitting in ninth position, showcased excellent attacking prowess as they downed the Magpies 2-1 at Hillsborough Stadium. Goals from Sam Hutchinson and Steven Fletcher proved to be the difference between the two sides, as Newcastle's attempts to mount a comeback fell short. Newcastle's star striker Dwight Gayle was once again forced to watch from the sidelines, picking up a fresh injury that added to his already considerable collection. The forward appeared to suffer achipf-break in Tuesday's warm-up ahead of the match, prompting concern among Newcastle's medical team. "He had a slight knock on his ankle, but didn't want to take any risks," Newcastle manager Rafael Benitez revealed post-match. "We'll need to assess the injury further, but it's definitely a concern for us." However it was Wednesday who seized control early on, as Hutchinson gave his side the lead in the 20th minute. The left-back unleashed a powerful strike, which arrowed into the top corner, leaving Newcastle goalkeeper Freddie Woodman with no chance. Newcastle struggled to find their rhythm after falling behind, with Gayle's absence clearly felt throughout the game. The Magpies created plenty of chances, but their finishing was wayward, with Woodman redeeming himself on numerous occasions to deny what looked like certain goals. The Owls doubled their lead just before halftime through Fletcher, who headed home a pinpoint delivery from target man Jordan Rhodes. With Wednesday 2-0 up at the break, Newcastle knew they needed to raise their game significantly if they were to have any hope of salvaging a point. And salvage a point is exactly what they did, getting one back through Florian Lejeune's well-placed header in the 62nd minute. However, despite Newcastle's best efforts, Wednesday's defence held firm to secure all three points and send a loud message to the rest of the Championship: they are a force to be reckoned with. Wednesday now lie just three points behind Rotherham in seventh, who have a crucial game against struggling Bolton this weekend. The Owls face off against fellow promotion hopefuls Derby at home next Saturday, but with a five-point cushion over the relegation zone, they will be confident that they can continue their charge towards the Championship play-offs.

A drunk driver who struck and killed a student has been handed a seven-year prison sentence. Daniel Ross, 30, was behind the wheel of a Land Rover when he collided with Sophie Jackson, 20, on a dark country lane in Wales in November 2018. The University of Exeter student, who was on a gap year volunteering group, died at the scene due to severe head injuries. Her parents, family and friends had called for a "life sentence" for Ross after he had admitted causing her death by careless driving while disqualified and drunk. The family, who had packed the court to hear the sentence, remained visibly emotional as the judge handed down the seven-year term at Cardiff Crown Court. Sophies' parents, Jo and Roy Jackson said after the sentencing that "knowing that justice has been done will give us some comfort with the pain of our loss but grief will not go away." A statement from the family continued: "Though seven years will pass, we will live with the loss of our beautiful daughter every day until we die. Just knowing that Daniel Ross's actions are punishable is more than we thought was ever possible. The public should be aware of the dangers of driving under the influence, especially heavy drinking and speeding, and I hopeSophie's life does not pass in vain. The report said: "He smelt heavily of intoxicating liquor, displayed signs of intoxication, denied he had been drinking, refused to participate in tests to assess the alcohol content of his breath and attempted to flee the scene." Carrying out a breath test Ross's reading rose above 120mg of alcohol in 100ml of blood he was released from £20 bail with £100 surety plus £20 court costs subject to appearing at the magistrates' first court on 28 November 2018.

British Cycling's medical services are set for a major overhaul following a scathing report by an independent panel, which has laid bare the organisational shortcomings that contributed to the tragic deaths of several elite riders, including 2012 Team Pursuit Olympic gold medallist and world champion Steven Burke's close friend, Neil Speakman. At the heart of the review, overseen by Sir Hugh Robertson, the former culture secretary, and chaired by Professor Nigel Jones, was an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of 31-year-old Speakman, a senior coach and rider development officer, who died suddenly in March last year at thechip data room in the Olympic park. But what unfolded was a far broader examination of British Cycling's handling of athlete welfare, highlighting the distressing fact that medical staff and officials were often unsure how to operate within the existing framework. The Future is Here: Virtual Reality Comes of Age Imagine a world where you can step into a movie, travel to exotic locations, and experience the thrill of adventure without leaving your living room. Sounds like science fiction? Not anymore. Virtual Reality (VR) technology has been around for decades, but the recent advancements have brought it to an unprecedented level of sophistication and accessibility. We're living in a brave new world where VR is no longer just a novelty, but a potential game-changer in various industries. The concept of Virtual Reality dates back to the 1960s, when computer scientist and engineer Morton Heilig designed the Sensorama, a head-mounted device that simulated a motorcycle ride. However, it wasn't until the 1980s and the advent of PC gaming that VR started to gain popularity. Games like "Flight Simulator" and "BattleZone" offered immersive experiences, but the technology was still clunky and expensive. Fast-forward to the 21st century, and VR has undergone a revolutionary transformation. The rise of consumer-grade VR headsets like Oculus Rift and HTC Vive has democratized access to this technology, making it possible for individuals to create and experience VR content at home. Today, VR is not just about gaming. It's being used in fields like education, healthcare, and entertainment to create engaging and interactive experiences. Students can explore virtual labs and classrooms, surgeons can practice complex operations in a simulated environment, and patients can undergo therapy in a controlled and safe space. The applications of VR are endless, and companies are starting to take notice. From tourism and travel companies to advertising agencies and event planners, many industries are exploring ways to harness VR's potential. However, as VR continues to advance, there are also concerns about its impact on society. Some experts warn about the potential risks of addiction, social isolation, and desensitization to violence. Additionally, there are questions about the need for new regulations and guidelines to ensure that VR technologies are used responsibly. As we enter this new era of VR, it's essential to ask: what does the future hold for this technology? Will VR become an integral part of our daily lives, or will it remain a niche interest? One thing is certain – the world will never be the same. The possibilities are endless, and as VR continues to evolve, we can expect to see even more innovative applications in the years to come.

The case centres on the defender's status as an international, and the document that he completed when he signed for Liverpool in 2016. According to reports, the document, which is required for every player moving from one country to Europe, did not mention that Matip would be playing for Liverpool. In Cameroon, where Matip hails from, the top-flight league is technically classified as a international championship. It is, therefore, understandable that Matip might not have considered Liverpool as a separate international club at the time of signing, opting to just check the box for playing for an international club. But, it appears, as Liverpool is a big club and FIFA doesn't understand "all these things", and certain interpretation of rules will move forward in different directions as understood by FIFA. However, all of this hinges around the club's submission of two pieces of paperwork, and, with the Reds having already submitted the first, all eyes now turn to whether the second will be accepted. If it is, and the disciplinary proceedings are dropped, Matip will be free to play for Liverpool but it is uncertain how he would fit in the league that he has started so well in and if Klopp will play with him or without him until this is all well resolved. The meeting will take place at the FIFA headquarters on Friday, and will see the representatives of Liverpool and Matip's attend an informal hearing to discuss the case. From there, the Disciplinary Committee will make a decision on the matter, which will have significant implications for the defender and the club. Regardless of the outcome, one thing is certain: Matip will have learned a valuable lesson about the intricacies of FIFA rules. He will now know that nothing short of 'absolute compliance' will deflect problems like this, no matter which rule books assure that you stay compliant.

US Regulators Give Final Approval to Volcker Rule Five years after being first proposed, the Volcker rule has finally received approval from all five US financial regulators, paving the way for its implementation and marking a significant step forward in the regulatory response to the 2008-09 financial collapse. Approved by the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the Volcker rule aims to restrict the use of taxpayer-insured deposits to fund high-risk trading activities, a key contributor to the financial crisis. The rule, named after former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker, was designed to ban banks from engaging in proprietary trading and hedge fund activities, which were seen as excessive and reckless in the run-up to the crash. Under the rule, banks will be allowed to engage in limited amounts of trading for hedging and market-making purposes, but will not be permitted to wager depositors' money in high-risk bets on the stock or bond markets. "We are pleased to see the final implementation of the Volcker rule, which is a key component of our post-crisis reforms," said Comptroller of the Currency Thomas Curry in a statement. "This rule is designed to protect taxpayers by preventing banks from engaging in potentially risky trading activities with insured deposits." The implementation of the Volcker rule is expected to result in significant changes to the way banks operate, and has been the subject of intense lobbying from the financial industry. While the rule is seen as a victory for regulators and consumer groups, banks have argued that it is overly complex and burdensome, and that it will make it more difficult for them to engage in legitimate market-making activities. In response to industry concerns, regulators have agreed to phase in the rule over a period of 13 months, allowing banks to adjust to the new requirements. The final rule also includes a number of exemptions and exceptions, including for certain types of trading activities and for banks with limited market-making capabilities. "The Volcker rule is an important step forward in our efforts to protect depositors and strengthen the banking system," said SEC Chairman Mary Jo White. "We believe that it will help to reduce the risks associated with proprietary trading and prevent the kind of systemic risk that led to the financial crisis."

The win catapulted Spurs into fourth spot, just a point behind third-placed Arsenal, and made it 10 matches unbeaten in the process. Harry Kane's strike on his 100th Tottenham appearance will be a memory he cherishes for a lifetime, but it was another inspired performance from the entire team that saw the visitors secure a hard-fought win. Ed Miliband has welcomed a strong performance from Labour in the European elections, despite the party coming second in the popular vote behind the Liberal Democrats. In a statement, Mr Miliband said that the election result showed Labour was "making progress" but acknowledged that there was still a way to go for the party to achieve success at the next general election. Liberal Democrat leader Tim Farron hailed his party's success as a "remarkable" and "overwhelming" victory for the party, with many of the seats they won having been previously held by other parties, including Labour and the Conservatives. "The European elections saw votes being driven by anti-immigrant sentiment and nationalism, and rather than just focusing on the practical things that Europe can do for people, we allowed the debate to be set by Nigel Farage and the UKIP, and the Remain campaigners," he said. UKIP leader Nigel Farage hailed the result as a "colossal" victory for his party, which he said had come from "nowhere". "I came into politics seven years ago with a rather quaint idea that the EU was the root of all our problems," he said.
