Irish fishermen made a jaws-dropping discovery last weekend when a gargantuan sixgill shark, estimated to be one of the largest caught in European waters, was hooked off the coast of County Clare. The sheer size of the creature sparked widespread amazement among marine biologists, with many experts hailing it as a once-in-a-lifetime catch. According to the Irish Charting Company, the sixgill shark measured 3.1 metres in length and weighed an astonishing 241 kilogrammes. For those unfamiliar, sixgill sharks are a relatively rare species found in deep waters worldwide, with the largest ever recorded measuring a staggering 6.4 metres in length. Shockingly, this colossal creature was caught using a smallish rod, raising serious questions about the suitability of recreational fishing gear for handling such massive beasts. The catch was made by two local fishermen, John Joyce and Mike Breen, off the Quilty coastline in County Clare. The men claimed the shark was thrashing violently, which complicated their efforts to land it safely. "I've been fishing for 40 years, and I've never seen anything like it," a still amazed Mr Joyce told our newspaper yesterday. "This must have been a marine monster, the likes of which few people have ever seen. It was fighting like a wild beast, which made it even harder to land. We knew we were in trouble as soon as the rod started bending, but I never thought it would be that big." Marine experts have since confirmed that this catch has set a new benchmark for the largest sixgill shark caught in Europe using a rod. "Sixgills are rarely recorded in Irish waters, and those that do appear are usually caught on baited hooks or by commercial trawlers," said Dr Simon Berrow, co-ordinator of the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group. "What we're seeing here is an extraordinary exception to the rule. No question, this was a massive animal." Marine scientists have been left scratching their heads trying to understand the reasons behind this extraordinary catch. "For a sixgill shark to appear in Irish waters, let alone fight its way up to the surface on a small rod, is nothing short of amazing," said Dr Chris Clark, an ichthyologist at University College Dublin. "Unless more research is done, we risk overlooking the complex patterns governing sixgill movements in this region." The catch has sent shockwaves across the water sports community, sparking heated debates about fisheries regulations and shark conservation.

As the tennis world gears up for the Australian Open, one question has dominated the conversation: Will Serena Williams finally usurp Steffi Graf's record of 22 Grand Slams? The American tennis superstar has consistently brushed off questions about the impact of Graf's record on her game. At a news conference in Melbourne, Williams confronted the issue head-on, once again expressing her ambivalence towards the milestone. "There's no distraction from trying to win the next tournament than trying to win any other tournament," she said firmly. When asked about whether she was motivated by the prospect of breaking Graf's record, Williams appeared to dismiss the idea altogether. "I think the only thing that matters to me is to go out there and play the best tennis I can. The rest will take care of itself." Despite her words, however, it's hard to imagine that Williams is not quietly focusing on the record. After all, it's a distinction that has eluded her for nearly two decades, with Graf maintaining the record since 1988. After winning 23 Grand Slams in 2017, Williams' very name is now inextricably linked to the metric. But when asked about how relevant the record is, especially given her various injuries and the current field of talented opponents, Williams chose to downplay the significance. She highlighted her determination to add to her trophy case at all costs, stating that she is focused on the sport itself: "You only know how good you are when you're out there competing." For many tennis fans, the prospect of witnessing a talent like Serena Williams break the record was a prospect they thought would never materialise. Graf's 22 Grand Slams made her an untouchable figure in tennis lore. But with a win in Melbourne, and by extension three more in the other Slams, Williams will finally move ahead of Graf's record. Says analyst Rudy Durbin, "Now is the chance for a female tennis player to surpass an incredible record from another era and feel worthy of it." Williams herself adds, "This tournament is not any more about that (record) any more than the US Open was. I try not to get my mind caught up in all those different thoughts and I just figure that the biggest challenge is to come out of here healthy." For sports observers like Mary Albuquerque, this deflective attitude encapsulates the winning mentality of Williams and that of a subjectivity desperately hopeful that the twilight of the world of sports will not be conquered based on sheer historical significance alone.

Flight BA292, flying from Mauritius to Heathrow Airport, was just 5 miles from the runway when the captain reported that the plane had suffered an "electrical fault" that had caused the aircraft to shake violently. However, an investigation is now under way to determine if the fault was caused by a collision with an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), or drone, that authorities believe was present in the landing path. The Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command has launched an investigation along with the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, which has raised serious concerns over the safety of commercial air travel. Dr Sarah Jones of the Aviation Safety Network described the incident as "very serious". "If a plane does collide with an object, such as a drone, then damage can be extensive, including potential damage to the engines and the airframe," she said. "The fact that the crew and passengers were able to land the plane safely is a testament to their skill and training. However, this does not diminish the severity of the incident in terms of safety, and the investigation into the cause of the electrical fault is ongoing." Drone sightings by pilots have become more frequent in recent years as the technology has become more widely available. However, these incidents have highlighted concerns over the lack of clear regulations and law enforcement in place to prevent drones from disrupting air navigation. The UK's aviation regulator, the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), claims it is "working closely" with law enforcement and partners to tackle the issue, but critics argue that too little has been done to tackle the threat posed by drones in near-air-space. Home Secretary Priti Patel has warned of the "deadly danger" posed by drones and has proposed tougher laws, including prison sentences and fines, for those found guilty of operating a drone in a way that recklessly endangers air traffic. The British Airline Pilots' Association (BALPA) has echoed those concerns, calling for tighter regulations and increased public awareness of the risks posed by drones near airports. "The incident at Heathrow is yet another reminder of the dangers posed by drones to the safety of our national airspace," said BALPA general secretary, Captain Conor McVeigh. "It's essential that we see a major crackdown on drone-related crime and increased public awareness of this critical threat." The CAA is urging anyone who has information about the incident, or who has witnessed the drone in the vicinity of Heathrow, to come forward.

Tragedy Struck the Aegean Sea as Migrant Disaster Claims Lives of at Least 27 A devastating scene has unfolded off the Turkish coast, where the bodies of at least 27 migrants were recovered after their makeshift vessel capsized in an attempt to cross the treacherous waters and reach the Greek island of Lesbos. Turkish media have reported that the migrants, believed to be Syrian nationals, were attempting to make the perilous journey in a rickety boat when it overturned, throwing countless souls into the unforgiving waters of the Aegean Sea. Eyewitnesses recounted the tragic events, describing the migrant vessel as taking on water mere metres off the Turkish coast. With no engine and no hope, the desperate passengers clung to the wreck as it began to sink beneath the waves. It is feared that more lives may have been lost in the disaster, with eyewitnesses reporting that survivors clung to the debris, screaming for help as Turkish coastguards arrived on the scene. Turkey's state-run news agency, Anadolu Agency, reported that the migrants had been spotted by local residents who had alerted authorities, who quickly dispatched a team of coastguards to the area. The relevant authorities claimed that the rescue operation is ongoing, though the risk of further loss of life remains high due to the seawater currents and the difficulty in locating bodies in the area. Greece has long been a despairing destination for thousands of migrants risking everything to escape war and economic devastation in their home countries. Between 2015 and 2016 alone, over 850,000 asylum-seekers arrived on the island of Lesbos, via the treacherous Aegean routes from Turkey. With ongoing conflict ravaging the Middle East and the enduring crisis that rippling across the region, it is feared that others will attempt the same treacherous journey, putting themselves at the mercy of the unforgiving sea. The incident has sparked a fresh wave of concern among international aid agencies and migration experts, who lament the strain placed on rescue services and local communities dealing with the humanitarian crisis unfolding in the region. "The grandfather of one child who was on the boat was killed during the fighting in Aleppo, and his family fled Syria seeking a better life," said Ayşe Tanoğlu, a prominent Turkish aid worker with a foundation focused on migrant relief. "These people have been sold false promises of a chance at a better future." Turkey's interior ministry stated on social media, mourning the dead, saying: "We offer our condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones in the boat accident while attempting to migrate to Greece."

Jailed for life after a brutal attack on 83 year old widow, Elizabeth Slater A man who subjected an 83-year-old widow to a horrific ordeal, leaving her tortured and battered to death with a rolling pin, has been convicted of her murder. Alan Hayes, 53, forced his way into Elizabeth Slater's home, demanding that she reveal her PIN number, and subjected her to a prolonged and violent attack. She died soon after at her home in Catford, south London, last November. The brutal nature of the crime prompted an outpouring of tributes for Mrs. Slater, with family, friends and neighbours paying tribute to her kind and gentle nature. Hayes, who was already known to Mrs. Slater through a acquaintanceship the court heard, was found guilty of her murder at the Old Bailey after a four-week trial. The court heard how Hayes, a violent and erratic individual with a history of violent offending, had forced his way into Mrs. Slater's home on November 25, demanding money from her. In a desperate bid to get what he wanted, Hayes turned violent, subjecting Mrs. Slater to a sustained attack. Prosecutors said he had "viciously" battered her with a rolling pin, causing severe head and facial injuries. A post-mortem examination later revealed that Mrs. Slater had suffered a severe head injury, including a fractured skull and bleeding to the brain, which led to her death. The jury was shown CCTV footage of Hayes leading Mrs. Slater from her front door to her kitchen, although the extremely violent event which took place in the kitchen, was not caught on camera. However, police were able to recover a bloody rolling pin and Hayes' DNA from the scene, which helped them link him to the crime. Hayes was arrested and charged with murder in December, and has been held on remand since then. The trial heard that Hayes had a history of violence and was known to police, with an expert witness from the probation service saying he posed a "high to very high risk of serious harm" to others. Sentencing Hayes to a minimum of 30 years in jail, Mr Justice Jeremy Baker described the attack as a "prolonged and brutal assault" that had resulted in "a completely horrific and unnatural death" for Mrs. Slater. He added: "It is clear that the defendant subjected Elizabeth Slater to a prolonged and brutal assault, culminating in the use of the rolling pin to cause her fatal injuries."

Plans to force all schools in England to become academies will be outlined in the Budget on Wednesday, in a move that has been met with concern from teachers and opposition politicians. The measures are part of a major shake-up of the country's education system, with Chancellor Philip Hammond expected to detail the government's plans in his Budget speech. The move follows a major review of education funding by Schools Minister Nick Gibb, who has been pushing for schools to be given more freedom to set their own budgets and make their own decisions. However, critics have warned that the plans will lead to a "two-tier" education system, where academies will receive more funding and have more autonomy than maintained schools. The National Union of Teachers (NUT) has condemned the plans, describing them as "a ideologically-driven attack on the education system". The union's general secretary, Kevin Courtney, said: "This is a prescription for chaos and would lead to the disintegration of the state education system. We cannot allow this to happen." Mike Farrar, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: "We are opposed to forcing schools to become academies. This is a top-down imposition and it will lead to more bureaucracy and more complexity." The opposition Labour Party has also lined up to criticise the plans, with Shadow Education Secretary Angela Rayner saying: "This is a botched attempt to privatise our education system. It will lead to a two-tier system, with some schools being forced to compete with each other for funding and resources." The plans are part of a wider review of the education system, which also includes proposals to increase funding for schools and to introduce new measures to prevent extremist ideologies from taking hold in education. Under the current system, schools are free to decide whether they want to become academies, but the government has been pushing hard to convert more schools to the academy model. There are now over 6,000 academies in England, but the government wants to see every school become an academy by 2022. This would mean that schools would be free from local authority control and would be able to set their own budgets and make their own decisions. However, critics have warned that this would lead to a lack of accountability and transparency, and would make it harder to identify and address underperforming schools.

Among the cramped streets and makeshift shops that line Cairo's bustling alleys, one establishment stands as a testament to tradition and innovation. In the heart of Ain Shams, a working-class neighbourhood that is home to some of the city's oldest and most resilient communities, is a humble shop that has been the go-to destination for Cairenes seeking something truly unique - gift wrapping and bespoke stationery. For over 60 years, Ahmed Ebrahim's Gift Wrapping Shop has offered an experience that is equal parts captivating and timeless. As you step off the chaotic streets and into the shop, the sounds of the outside world melt away, replaced by the aroma of aged paper and the soft rustling of crisp new packages. With its faded sign and worn wooden exterior, the shop doesn't seem to boast much from the outside, but venture inside and you'll discover a veritable treasure trove of craftsmanship and artistry. Ebrahim's family has been perfecting the art of gift wrapping for generations, with skills passed down from father to son like a precious heirloom. The shop itself is an Aladdin's cave of beautiful, handmade boxes crafted from the finest Egyptian paper, adorned with intricate designs and patterns that showcase the skill of Ebrahim's team of expert paper-crafters. As you browse the aisles, you will find not only an impressive selection of beautifully wrapped gifts but also a dizzying array of custom-made stationery - invitations, greeting cards, and even bespoke notebooks that cater to every taste and occasion. For decades, Cairo's elite and middle classes have sought Ebrahim's expert services for special occasions such as weddings, Ramadan celebrations and new year festivities. The shop also caters to diplomats, politicians and ambassadors who are drawn to its unique custom-made notebooks and folders. Today, gift wrapping has become a lost art in the age of digital consumerism, where packages arrive wrapped in the most basic of materials and are often discarded after a single use. In an era where people increasingly rely on ubiquitous online retailers, Ebrahim's Gift Wrapping Shop stands as a defiantly old-fashioned beacon of hope, offering something far more meaningful to the shopper - a chance to own a part of its history, literally wrapped up in a beautiful package. As our visit draws to a close, it is clear that this unassuming shop on this unassuming street holds far greater significance than meets the eye - a small but determined voice in the crowd of omnipresent chain stores that dominate every city centre.

The manifesto, titled "Prosperity, Justice and the Voice of the People: A Programme for Government in Wales", is a comprehensive document that outlines the party's vision for a renovated Welsh economy, a more sustainable environment and a more equal society. One of the centrepieces of the manifesto is the promise of an independent Welsh government having control over its own finances. Plaid Cymru argues that the current system, which sees Westminster retain control of tax and borrowing, denies Wales the autonomy to make its own decisions and to invest in the things that matter most. According to the manifesto, an independent Welsh government would be able to raise its own income tax rate, as well as wages and capital gains tax, allowing for greater flexibility and a more targeted approach to taxation. This, the party says, would enable the Welsh government to raise more than £1 billion extra, which could be spent on public services, infrastructure and job creation. Furthermore, the manifesto outlines a range of policies aimed at boosting the Welsh economy, including a major investment in renewable energy, a £100 million fund to support small businesses and entrepreneurs, and a new approach to industrial policy that would focus on developing Wales' unique strengths and capabilities. On the environment, Plaid Cymru promises to take action to protect Wales' natural beauty, including the restoration of forests, the creation of a Welsh green investment bank and the establishment of a new national park in the north of the country. The manifesto also outlines a commitment to social justice, including a £10 per hour minimum wage, the abolition of prescription charges and the establishment of a Welsh care and support system. On the devolution of powers, Plaid Cymru proposes the transfer of new powers from Westminster to the Welsh Assembly, including control over employment law and workers' rights, the establishment of a new public body to oversee NHS Wales and greater powers to regulate the housing market. While the details of the manifesto are undoubtedly ambitious, the stakes this May are no less important.

In his final appearance at the despatch box for prime minister's questions, David Cameron gave a defiant defence of his legacy on Northern Ireland, claiming that the region was "stronger now than when I came to power six years ago". The outgoing Prime Minister made the statement in response to a question from the DUP's Nigel Dodds, who praised Mr Cameron for his gift of the Irish language title to the Queen, but criticised his record on the welfare reform bill. Mr Cameron said: "I think one of the things that I'm most proud of is the progress that has been made in Northern Ireland over the past six years. "When I came into office, there was still a great deal of uncertainty and unfinished business from the peace process, but I think we've made progress on that and the region is stronger now than when I came to power." The Prime Minister cited his government's role in the Stormont House Agreement and the Fresh Start deal as examples of this progress, but the DUP's Mr Dodds was quick to point out that the legacy of these deals in terms of the provision of services is more relevant than the agreement itself. He went on: "If I could, I'd ask the Prime Minister a question, and notwithstanding his answer I'd like to make a comment to him. "PT appointments, for example, have been vacant for 3,107 days in one trust. Is that the kind of progress that he wants to leave behind?" As the session came to a close, Mr Cameron reflected on his own record on Northern Ireland, acknowledging that the peace process was a complex and difficult topic. He also echoed his comments in a speech at the Queen's university earlier this week, when he warned against the dangers of the past being repeated in the present and future. The Prime Minister said: "Twenty years ago, the IRA was waging a terrorist campaign against innocent people, and the Union was still very much at risk. "We've seen an end to that campaign, and indeed the decommissioning of all the main paramilitary groups. We've seen runs of succession without shots being fired. But let's be clear: that was hard work, that was progress, and that is not to be taken for granted. "We shouldn't be looking to the future by going back to the past."

University Students Awarded £400,000 in Compensation A recent Freedom of Information request has revealed that universities in England and Wales paid out £400,000 in compensation to students last year alone. The figures, obtained by university watchdog, Which?, shine a light on the prevalence of complaints made by students, and the sometimes hefty sums required to resolve them. The data, which covers the period from 2022 to 2023, shows that universities in both England and Wales made a total of 245 payments to students, with the highest single payment reaching £36,000. Although these payments are often reported to be for breach of contract, the reasons behind the complaints are often more complex. The £400,000 total is a significant increase from 2021, when universities paid out £240,000 to students. Experts believe that this rise may be attributed to the ongoing student accommodation crisis, as well as increased awareness and confidence among students to report issues to their universities. We spoke to Sarah Jones, a third-year student at the University of Birmingham, who received a payment of £2,000 from her university after reporting issues with her accommodation. "I had chosen to live in halls of residence, thinking it would be a great experience, but I ended up with a room in a shared flat that was plagued by cleanliness and noise problems," she explained. "It was really frustrating, and I'm glad I got some compensation for it." However, not all students who make complaints are successful in securing payments. We spoke to James Wilson, a final-year student at the University of Lancaster, who was left feeling frustrated after being denied compensation for accommodation issues. "I had a meeting with the university's resolver team, but they just didn't seem to take my concerns seriously," he said. "It was really disheartening, and I felt like my voice wasn't being heard." Universities in England and Wales have come under fire in recent years for their handling of student complaints. A 2022 report by the National Student Survey found that, despite improvements in overall student satisfaction, many students felt that their concerns were not being taken seriously. In response to the data, Which? has called for universities to be more transparent about their complaint-handling processes and to ensure that students are adequately supported throughout the resolution process. "Students have the right to expect a high-quality education and a fair deal when it comes to their accommodation and other university services," said a spokesperson for the organisation.

Scottish Government Rules Out Return of Post-Study Work Visa, Causes Outrage Among International Students A decision by the Scottish Government to reject calls for the reintroduction of a post-study work visa system for international students has sparked outrage among thousands of students who rely on the visa to remain in Scotland after completing their studies. The news comes as a major blow to many international students who had been hoping to extend their stay in Scotland to gain work experience and build their careers. The student visa system, which previously allowed international students to work for up to two years after graduating, was abolished in 2012 by the UK Government as part of a broader crackdown on immigration. The Scottish National Party (SNP) administration, led by First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, has long been under pressure to reinstate the post-study work visa system, which was a key feature of the old student visa policy. Many had hoped that the SNP would take advantage of Scotland's new powers in immigration policy, introduced as a result of the devolution of more powers from Westminster, to bring in a more student-friendly immigration regime. However, speaking at the Scottish Parliament, the Scottish Government's Migration Minister, Ben Macpherson, made it clear that the SNP was not prepared to reintroduce the post-study work visa. Macpherson, said: "I understand that some international students wish to stay in Scotland after completing their studies. However, we cannot simply reinstate a system that was revoked by the UK Government. Our focus is on creating jobs and growing our economy, and we will do so without artificially extending the right to work for international students." The Minister's comments have been met with anger from many international students, who argue that the SNP's decision will make it much harder for them to build their careers in Scotland. According to Scottish universities, there are over 15,000 international students currently studying in the country, with thousands more expected to arrive in the coming year. Many international students are now facing the prospect of having to return home or to other parts of the UK after graduating, which runs the risk of losing valuable skills and expertise that could be important to Scotland's economic future. The decision has also been criticised by free market think-tanks and business leaders, who argue that restricting the mobility of international students will make Scotland less attractive to students from around the world.

He described their plan as a "very complex" one involving the use of fake identities, and "complex financial arrangements" to bring the guns into the country. The guns, which were worth tens of thousands of pounds, had been brought in from Europe through various routes and packages. Two other men, Styopan Patitsas and Moses Oduor, had pleaded guilty earlier, and Dmitry Ustinov was still being investigated in Russia over his alleged role in the gang. Det Supt Horton said: "This is a significant result and it is all thanks to the hard work of the officers dealing with this case. The National Health Service (NHS) is to face a major shake-up, with the head of the health service announcing that nearly 20% of NHS trusts in England will be placed in special measures due to persistent problems with care standards. NHS chief executive, Amanda Pritchard, made the announcement, revealing that trusts will be subject to increased scrutiny and support in a bid to tackle failings in services. Special measures have been used successfully in the past to turn around ailing services, but it is a rare and severe intervention, typically reserved for trusts that have been identified as 'inadequate' by the Care Quality Commission (CQC). Under the new measures, NHS trusts with the most pressing issues will face increased intervention and support from NHS England and the CQC, including more frequent inspections and the deployment of an expert team to help with improvement. Trusts will also be required to submit regular reports on their progress and will face significant action if they fail to show improvement. Mrs. Pritchard stressed that the decision to place trusts in special measures was not a criticism, but an opportunity to bring in greater support to tackle the underlying issues driving poor care. The environment has been granted a reprieve of sorts till now, thanks in large part to individuals and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) willing to take action in the courts to protect it. However, new rules that came into force today are set to fundamentally change the game. Judicial review, a crucial tool in environmental law that has been used to hold governments and corporations to account for their actions, is being significantly curtailed. Under the new rules, claimants will have to show a "sufficient interest" in a case to be eligible to bring a judicial review, rather than the more relaxed threshold that previously applied. While the idea of "standing" in a case may sound technical, its impact will be far-reaching. "It's going to create a huge barrier for people who want to bring cases on an environmental basis," says veteran environmental lawyer, Helena Mills. "Unless you're directly affected by the decision, I don't think you'll be able to challenge it." For example, if a pollution hotspot affects an entire community, under the new rules only those living immediately next to the site may be able to bring a case. Everyone else may be left to suffer in silence. The changes have been made under the Domestic Revenue Taxation (DRD) regulations, which were introduced by the Ministry of Justice. The Ministry insists that the reforms are necessary to "improve the efficiency" of the judicial review system. However, environmental experts are warning that the impact will be devastating. "It's a knee-jerk reaction by the Ministry of Justice to sort out some alleged judicial review 'abuse'" says Dr. Andrew Morgan, Head of the Environmental Law Research Centre at the University of Exeter. "But what it will actually do is silence the voices of the quiet activists who are most keen to protect the environment." In recent years, judicial review has been a powerful tool for the environment, with campaigners using the courts to challenge decisions that would lead to major developments such as fracking sites and large-scale wind farms. However, the changes, which were announced in the spring, have far-reaching implications for anyone who wants to use the courts to try and protect the environment. "It will be much harder for NGOs to bring cases now," says Mills. "That's where the battle is going to be played out." Environmental groups this week wrote to the Ministry of Justice, demanding that they withdrew the regulations and threw them out.

In a major breakthrough, a new Palestinian unity government has been sworn in, bringing an end to nearly a decade of division and infighting between the rival factions of Hamas and Fatah. The move comes as a significant step towards healing the bitter rift that has crippled Palestinian politics and crippled the Palestinian Authority (PA). The Hamas-Fatah split, which emerged in 2007, led to the formation of two separate governments: one in the Gaza Strip, ruled by Hamas, and the other in the West Bank, led by Fatah. The division was marked by violence, including a bloody clash in Gaza City in 2007 that left many Gazans without basic necessities like water, electricity, and jobs. The long-awaited unity government, formed through a series of secret talks between Hamas and Fatah, was headed by Prime Minister Mohammed Ishtayeh, a seasoned diplomat and top Fatah official, and took the oath of office earlier today in Ramallah, the seat of the PA. Ishtayeh stressed the importance of "giving priority to the Palestinian people's interests and their rights, primarily to the right of return and the right to establish an independent Palestinian state" with East Jerusalem as its capital. This unity government brings together a 24-member cabinet comprising Hamas and Fatah members, as well as independents. While the new government is a crucial development towards re-uniting the West Bank and Gaza, Ramallah, and Gaza under one authority, its formation will be subject to international approval and scrutiny. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas hailed the new government, saying it was a "historic step" that would help reunify the Palestinian territories. The United States, a long-time ally of Israel and a critical backer of the Palestinian Authority, welcomed the unity government, albeit cautiously. Spokesman for the US Department of State, Ned Price praised "the commitment by the Palestinian Authority to reconciliation with Hamas and support for a sovereign and an independent Palestine", and said the US is prepared to engage in efforts to promote a lasting peace. However, given Washington's conflicts with both Hamas and Iran, it remains to be seen whether US aid to the Palestinian Authority will return to its pre-massive crisis levels. Meanwhile, sources within Hamas indicated that they are eager to exchange detained Palestinian prisoners with Israeli captives this year. Hugo Burge, the chair of Kick It Out, a UK-wide organisation aimed at tackling racism in football, made the call in an interview with BBC Sport. Mr Burge said that League One and League Two clubs must "take proactive steps" to address the lack of diversity in the profession. Currently, only six of the 92 clubs in the English Football League have a BAME manager. Mr Burge said: "If you're not actively trying to encourage a diverse pool of candidates, then you're unlikely to get a diverse pool of candidates. "We're not saying that you've got to appoint one, but at least give the opportunity to the people who have got the skills, the passion and the dedication to be a part of the game." He added that sanctions should be considered if clubs do not meet these demands, stating that the current system is "rhetorical" and does not lead to meaningful change: "If the league doesn't do it, we will call for action. "We've been talking about this for too long; it's not working. We've got to move towards, not just words, but actions." Kick It Out is working with the relevant authorities to "not just set guidelines, but also the teeth to enforce those guidelines". Mr Burge did acknowledge that some clubs were making efforts to improve diversity, but expressed frustration at those who were not. He highlighted the examples of Luton Town and Tranmere Rovers, who had made significant progress in appointing BAME players to coaching roles. At present, the EFL does not have formal guidelines on diversity for coaching appointments. The association does, however, have a leadership group made up of chief executive officers from clubs, that welcomes discussions on the topic. Mr Burge stressed that improved diversity would not only be good for the football industry but also for the wider society: "We shouldn't just be talking about players; let's talk about the coaching staff, the management, the technical staff and the administrators. "We need to make sure, across the board, that we've got people from all walks of life and that we're a true reflection of the community that we serve." Mobile Phone Roaming Deals a Victory for Travellers as EU Proposes Major Changes to Data Charges Travellers will now be able to continue using their mobile phones without incurring excessive data charges when roaming in Europe, as proposed new rules scrap planned time limits on surcharge-free roaming. The decision, announced by the European Commission, aims to ensure that EU citizens and businesses can stay connected when abroad without being hit with unexpectedly high bills. Under the original plans, regulators had set a daily cap on roaming data usage in order to prevent individuals from exceeding a certain limit and incurring incur high data charges. However, the European Commission has now scrapped this idea, citing concerns that the limit would cause inconvenience for users who need to stay online for extended periods while abroad. "The Commission is committed to protecting consumers and ensuring that EU citizens can benefit from digital opportunities while abroad," said Commissioner for Digital Economy and Society, Mariya Gabriel. "The absurd situation where people couldn't access data for extended periods without running into unforeseen costs is a thing of the past." The changes mean that from June next year, the EU will increase the cap on roaming data charges to a still to be revealed GB limit, after Brexit it will rise to 45 euros ($51), based on the current 45GB cap and averaged EU-wide charge, down from 60 euros ($69), after Brexit. However, there'll also be no additional restrictions for recipients of roaming communications such as text and voice messages, that'll remain unlimited. This is a win for those constantly on the move for both business and personal reasons. The Commission's decision is the latest step in a long-running effort to liberalise telecommunications across the bloc. In recent years, roaming charges have been almost completely abolished, with data and voice rates being largely equalised across the EU. While the plans will undoubtedly deliver a welcome boost to travellers' mobile plans, the changes also throw into sharp relief the thorny issue of Britain's impending departure from the EU. Until Brexit is complete, it will remain to be seen whether new UK roaming rates will come into effect or indeed if any grandfathered deals will stay in place. This will then certainly be clarified once Brexit is complete, after free movement has ceased. As the clock ticks down to 2021, one thing is certain: this piece of legislation does this much needed move, at the right time for millions that travel annually.

A devastating verdict for Bollywood superstar Salman Khan yesterday as an Indian court ruled that he will face a charge of culpable homicide for his role in a hit-and-run incident over a decade ago. The high-profile case has been marred by controversy and delay, with Khan, 52, accused of driving his car over five people sleeping on a pavement in Bandra, Mumbai, in September 2002. One man, Nurul Haq, died in the incident, while the four others injured survived. Khan, who has a reputation for being one of India's most wealthy and influential celebrities, maintained his innocence throughout the trial and claimed that he had fallen asleep at the wheel. However, the prosecution presented evidence that Khan had been driving under the influence of alcohol and had lost control of his car, hitting the sleeping men. Khan was initially charged with causing death by negligence, but yesterday the magistrate's court in Mumbai increased the charge to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, which is a more serious offense. Khan is likely to face a significant prison sentence if convicted in the higher court, although the exact punishment is difficult to predict at this stage. The case has been highly publicised in India and Bollywood, with many of Khan's fans expressing support for their beloved star. However, the incident and subsequent trial have sparked widespread outrage and calls for justice to be served. "We have been waiting for this verdict for 10 years," said Shahid Bal, a lawyer representing the victims' families. "We are happy that the court has finally taken cognisance of the accused's negligence and has enhanced the charge." Yesterday's verdict was seen as a significant development in the case, and is likely to send shockwaves throughout the Bollywood industry. Khan has been a dominant force in Indian cinema for decades, starring in some of the country's most successful and iconic films. He has also been a vocal advocate for various social causes, including animal welfare and poverty reduction. However, the ongoing court case has put Khan's reputation at the forefront of the public's consciousness, forcing the actor to address questions about his character and personal conduct. The hit-and-run incident is a serious stain on Khan's otherwise impressive public image, and it remains to be seen how this ruling will affect his future in the entertainment industry.

With over a quarter of a million children living in poverty in Scotland, many are relying on school meals as their main source of nutrition. However, with budgets being stretched to the limit, the quality and availability of free school meals are under threat. The National Union of Students has expressed its concerns over the issue, suggesting that some pupils are even resorting to stealing food from classmates due to desperation. It's estimated that nearly 230,000 children in Scotland are living below the poverty line, with one in five children from disadvantaged backgrounds struggling to access healthy meals. While the Scottish Government has committed to providing an extra £23 million to support families in poverty, schools are facing significant challenges in ensuring that every pupil gets the food they need to succeed. "We've had a number of instances where pupils have been stealing food from their classmates," said a teacher in Glasgow. "It's heartbreaking to see, especially when you know that they're doing it out of desperation." Ministers have vowed to address the issue but admitted they face significant challenges. A Government spokesperson said: "We know that certain pupils in Scotland are struggling with hunger, and as a result, their ability to learn and engage in school is being affected." However, while expressions of concern and promises of support are welcome, some ask what tangible steps can be taken to alleviate the problem. Teachers and charities call for a radical rethink of the childcare system in Scotland. The Minister said that improving childcare pay would lift many a clan out of poverty. First Minister Sturgeon welcomes the calls for a review and added the problems around food vouchers are limited due to their lack of availability and restrictions on who receives them. This demonstrates that current policies are unable to tackle child hunger. In a bid to address the issue, parents and youngsters are visiting the schools' kitchen to find out what children are eating. National charities also running initiatives to help families struggling to put food on the table. Angela Constance, Scotland's Minister for Children and Young People, has agreed to hold talks with the charity Age Scotland and others to "drive forward" solutions.

Operation Sunrise: Tackling FGM in the UK In a major crackdown on a deeply disturbing practice, police forces across the UK are joining forces to combat the issue of girls being taken out of the country for Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). The operation, dubbed Operation Sunrise, is a concerted effort to identify and disrupt the group's travel plans and to work with victims and their families to ensure their safety. FGM is a brutal and inhumane practice that involves the partial or total removal of a girl's external genitalia, often performed in secret and without her consent. The practice is most commonly carried out in countries in Africa and the Middle East, where it is deeply rooted in cultural and social tradition. However, with an estimated 137,000 girls under the age of 15 at risk of FGM in the UK alone, authorities have been working to combat the trend of UK-born girls and women being taken abroad for the procedure. Operation Sunrise is a response to the growing concern that girls are being targeted by individuals and groups who seek to subject them to FGM. Police forces will be working closely with social services, healthcare providers, and other agencies to identify potential victims and their families, as well as those who may be arranging for the girls to travel to countries where FGM is common. "We know that FGM is a deeply entrenched issue, but we also know that we can make a real difference by working together with the community, with healthcare providers, and with the girls and their families themselves," said a senior police officer involved in the operation. As part of the operation, officers will be working to gather intelligence on groups and individuals involved in arranging FGM, as well as on the routes that these individuals typically take. They will also be engaging with communities across the country to raise awareness of the dangers of FGM and to encourage parents and guardians to seek help if they suspect that their child is at risk. The police are aware that FGM is often performed in countries with weaker laws and stricter social norms, where victims are often reluctant to come forward for fear of being ostracized by their families or communities. In these environments, the procedure is often perpetrated in secret, with the individuals involved denying that the practice is taking place. However, Operation Sunrise is a determined effort to shine a light on this hidden practice and to bring perpetrators to justice.

Innocent People Wrongly Detained: Communication Data Errors a Major Concern, Say Watchdogs A devastating report by the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) and the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary (JT) suggests that up to 13 innocent people were wrongly arrested due to errors in the use of communication data by UK authorities. The group, comprising of senior judges and an independent reviewer of terrorism legislation, discovered that police and intelligence agencies made mistakes in obtaining and using data from communications service providers. The report, published on Monday, exposes serious flaws in the way communication data is processed and used by law enforcement agencies. According to the findings, many of the errors stem from incorrect or incomplete information provided by police, intelligence agencies, or communications service providers. This, in turn, led to innocent individuals being subjected to unnecessary detention, interrogation, and even prosecution. One of the cases highlighted by the report involves a man who was detained in 2016 after an incorrect match was found between his mobile phone number and an individual known to be linked to terrorism. He was held for several hours, only to be later released without charge after it became clear that the connection was a mere coincidence. "This is a shattering case of heavy-handed policing, where the risk of wrongful detention is a stark reminder of the dangers of operating on incomplete or inaccurate information," said a spokesperson for the IPT. "These mistakes undermine public trust in the justice system and further highlight the need for greater safeguards and accountability." The report's findings have led to renewed calls for greater transparency and oversight in the use of communication data by UK authorities. Many are calling for an independent review of the existing system, which has been in place since the passage of the Investigatory Powers Act in 2016. "This report highlights the problems we've warned about for years," said a spokesperson for the watchdog group, Liberty. "We've continually pressed the authorities to improve their processes and ensure that innocent people are not caught in the net of dragnet surveillance. This is a crucial moment to take stock and address these concerns." The IPT's report comes at a time when concerns about the use of communication data by UK authorities are already running high. Human rights groups, civil liberties organizations, and opposition MPs have long expressed concern about the potential risks of mass surveillance, particularly in the context of the Investigatory Powers Act.

Scientists say they have made a significant leap towards creating a vaccine that would protect against every form of flu, with a groundbreaking new discovery that could potentially revolutionise the way the NHS deals with winter illnesses. Researchers at Imperial College London have identified the key elements that make up the genetic blueprints of all 18 flu viruses, paving the way for the development of a universal vaccine that can protect against every strain of the virus. According to Dr. Kotsuma Yamayoshi, a lead researcher on the project, understanding the genetic makeup of the flu viruses is a crucial step towards creating a vaccine that can provide long-term protection against the virus. "Our approach is to study the viral genetic material, the genome, of all flu viruses," he explained. "This will allow us to identify the similarities and differences between the viruses, which will ultimately lead to the development of a universal vaccine that can protect against all types of flu." The team used a cutting-edge technique called " single-molecule fluorescence microscopy" to sequence the genomes of 18 different flu viruses. They found that all flu viruses share a number of key genetic features, which can be targeted with a vaccine. The breakthrough is highly significant, as it could lead to a vaccine that can provide protection against all forms of flu, including pandemic strains that cause widespread illness. Currently, the flu vaccine is only effective against the dominant strain of the virus that has been identified before the previous winter. This means that only 50-60% of flu viruses are protected against by the vaccine. If a universal flu vaccine can be developed, it could provide near-total protection, significantly reducing the burden on the NHS and saving countless lives. "The potential impact of this discovery could be enormous," said Dr. Yamayoshi. "If we can develop a universal flu vaccine, it could be a game-changer for public health. We could finally have a way to protect against the flu that is effective against all types of the virus." The team's findings were published in the journal Science, and have been hailed as a major breakthrough by the World Health Organisation (WHO). While the discovery is a significant step towards a universal flu vaccine, more work is needed to develop a vaccine that is both safe and effective. However, with the global health outlook looking increasingly bleak, the prospect of a 'one-size-fits-all' vaccine is a welcome one.

Poland's Pisa Effect: The Education Miracle That Shocked the World Ten years is a long time in the education sector, but it's a blink of an eye when it comes to the meteoric rise of Poland's pupils in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's (OECD) Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) tests. Between 2000 and 2012, Poland transformed its education system, producing astonishing results that have left experts and policymakers around the world stunned. In the 2000 Pisa tests, Polish pupils ranked a modest 24th among participating countries in mathematics, 26th in reading, and 21st in science. Fast forward to 2012, and Poland's rankings had catapulted to 14th in mathematics, 16th in reading, and 10th in science. The improvement was nothing short of remarkable, with many considering it one of the greatest in the history of the Pisa tests. But what exactly drove this cambio? Prior to the 1990s, the Polish education system was characterised by a high level of centralisation, with a rigid curriculum and teaching methods that left little room for innovation. However, in the early 2000s, Poland embarked on a major reform of its education system, introducing sweeping changes aimed at increasing transparency, accountability, and student autonomy. One key change was the introduction of modular exams, which allowed pupils to take individual components of the curriculum at different stages of their education, rather than in a single, high-stakes exam at the end of their schooling. This not only reduced stress levels but also allowed pupils to focus on areas where they needed improvement, paving the way for more tailored learning experiences. Another crucial move was the creation of regional education boards, which were tasked with improving teacher training, introducing new teaching methods, and developing more sophisticated assessment tools. By decentralising power, Polish policymakers were able to tap into local expertise and knowledge, fostering more effective collaboration between educators, parents, and policymakers. Poland's remarkable transformation was also underpinned by a sustained commitment to teacher training and development. The country invested heavily in professional development programmes for educators, providing them with the skills and confidence they needed to deliver high-quality instruction and adapt to changing educational landscapes. The impact of these reforms was felt far beyond the classroom. By 2012, Polish schools had become hubs of community activity, where parents and local business leaders were actively involved in shaping educational policy and fostering partnerships with schools.

In a rare show of unity among some of the sector's most influential figures, Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Twitter's Jack Dorsey, and eBay's Pierre Omidyar have joined forces to condemn a proposed US law that critics say could severely limit online freedom of expression. The Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) proposed legislation, known as the Climate-Related Finanacial Disclosure Rule, has sparked outrage among tech entrepreneurs and civil liberties groups. The proposed law would compel publicly traded companies to disclose their environmental, social, and governance (ESG) data to investors and regulators. Critics argue the legislation risks infringing on companies' First Amendment rights and opening the door to censorship of online content. In a strongly worded letter to the SEC, the group of venture capitalists and tech moguls expressed "deep concerns" about the legislation, arguing it marks a "significant step towards government-regulated content and would fundamentally alter the way that American companies can engage with the public on matters of serious public concern." The letter also warns that "artificially coupling a company's business performance to their perceived 'stewardship performance' poses a significant risk to the free and open conduct of business." Critics of the legislation claim it is overly broad and ill-defined, potentially giving regulators and courts too much discretion over what types of speech are considered acceptable. "This rule is a prime example of how misguided overregulation can undermine both transparency and accountability, and should be rejected outright," the founders wrote. The letter comes ahead of a Senate committee hearing next week, which is set to debate the proposed rule and consider potential amendments. The CEOs' unified stance is a rare but significant intervention by influential figures in the tech world, who often prefer to operate behind the scenes rather than engaging in public controversy. The move reflects growing concerns within the industry about the potential impact of overregulation on online speech and the delicate balance between corporate responsibility and First Amendment protections. Furthermore, major companies including Amazon and Microsoft have also voiced their opposition to the proposal. The founders of Google, Twitter and eBay have made it clear that any grandfathering provision that might be included in the final draft would not be enough to alleviate their concerns. They are calling on the SEC to withdraw the proposal and engage with the tech industry and civil society organisations to reach a more balanced and practical solution to the complex issues surrounding climate-related disclosures that doesn't undermine openness and access to markets.

Plaid Cymru has reiterated its call for the Welsh Government to increase the priority it gives to teaching the Welsh language, in an effort to help meet its target of one million Welsh speakers by 2050. The party's policy paper, launched yesterday, argues that unless urgent action is taken to reverse the decline in the language, the government's ambitious target is unlikely to be achieved. Official statistics show that the number of Welsh speakers peaked in 2004 at around 582,000, but has been decreasing ever since. There are thought to be around 562,000 people who are able to speak the language. According to the paper, many of the opportunities for learning Welsh being discussed by ministers would only benefit existing Welsh speakers. It claims that the majority of primary schools in Wales no longer offer Welsh as a first language choice for new entrants. In fact, by 2018, over 50% of primary schools in the capital city of Cardiff offered it, down from 91% in 2002/3. The party argues that a shift in priorities and a concerted effort to make more opportunities available, including greater use of the language in education, is needed. "Plaid Cymru believes that we can help ensure the growth of the Welsh language, especially in the early years of education, and move towards our goal of a million Welsh speakers by 2050," the paper states. Under the party's proposals, the Welsh Government would require all primary schools to offer Welsh first language classes to pupils whose families wish them to do so. They also call for an end to the "Teaching for Mastery" project in maths, which has been widely but not unanimously praised, to free up resources to promote Welsh language teaching.
